title: Air Is Easing Out of the AI Bubble
text:
Updated at 10:20 a.m. ET on November 23, 2026 

 This should be a bullish time for investors in the AI business. Nvidia, which designs most of the chips that have driven the AI boom, just reported that its sales and profits doubled year-over-year, and that it’s on pace to grow another 75 percent next year. The industry as a whole, Nvidia said, has a backlog of $2.5 trillion in future orders, meaning that demand remains strong. Anthropic, one of the industry’s two dominant developers of large language models, went public on Thursday and raised more money in its IPO than any company in history.

 Yet the dominant mood among investors is a sense of deep anxiety, not to say panic. Last Thursday, stocks soared when the market opened, buoyed by Anthropic’s debut. But by late morning, investors started selling, and by the end of the day the market was down more than 2 percent. On Friday, stocks sold off even more sharply, leaving the tech-heavy Nasdaq in negative territory for the year.

 AI companies are still collectively worth many trillions of dollars, but investors are looking at them, for the first time, with a more jaundiced eye. This is in part due to developments that few anticipated. The scandal at Nvidia , in which its founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was forced to suddenly step down after revelations of multiple affairs, including one with a possible Chinese intelligence asset, has created turmoil at the company that has almost single-handedly propped up the entire AI industry. (The company unexpectedly reinstated him this morning, apparently thanks in part to President Trump’s advocacy on Huang’s behalf. Investors greeted the news by bidding up not just Nvidia's stock but tech stocks generally, which underscores the volatility of the market.) The Democrats’ massive victory in the midterms has also sparked doubt about the future of AI development. Many Democrats ran on a platform of slowing or even prohibiting the construction of AI data centers—an approach that resonated with voters, according to exit polls, and promises new political headwinds for the sector.

 [ Read: The scandal is bigger than Jensen Huang ] 

 Even before Election Day and Huang’s unceremonious exit, a fundamental shift in the market’s attitude toward AI companies was under way. Since OpenAI released ChatGPT in 2022, investors have blithely poured money into the AI business on the assumption that somewhere down the road, it would become very profitable. Tech giants themselves have adopted the same strategy. Companies such as Google and Meta have spent hundreds of billions of dollars to build out their AI capabilities. But the sums of money required for this build-out are so immense—and the prospects for profit still so distant—that investors have, of late, become more demanding and less patient.

 At the moment, most of the money being spent on AI is being spent by AI companies, whether they’re constructing data centers or buying GPUs and memory chips from manufacturers or compute power from hyperscalers. There is a circularity to the business, whereby many of the companies in the industry are investing in and financing one another, while also selling to or buying from, or even competing with, one another. Earlier this year, Nvidia invested $30 billion in OpenAI, which in turn bought Nvidia chips. Anthropic, meanwhile, buys chips from Google, which is also one of its biggest investors—and one of its biggest rivals.  

 There’s nothing wrong with this. When railroads were being built across the United States, much of the money came from companies in the rail industry. The same was true when the country electrified homes and industry. This is the nature of a massive build-out of infrastructure with anticipated future benefits.

 The key, though, is that in order for a build-out to be profitable—which is what investors care about—customers outside the industry will need to start spending huge sums on the product. This can take time; it took close to 30 years after the big commercial-rail build-out started for railroads to become sustainably profitable. In the case of AI, the sums necessary to turn a profit are truly huge. A number of recent studies estimate that AI revenues will have to exceed $3.5 trillion a year or more by 2032 just for companies to earn a 10 percent return on all the capital expenditures they’ve made so far.

 [ Read: The reluctant winner of the AI race ] 

 If AI ends up radically reinventing entire industries, such as pharmaceuticals, these numbers are not impossible. But at the moment, it’s hard to see where all of that additional revenue would come from. Anthropic, for instance, has built a strong business licensing its LLMs; the company is currently on track to earn more than $80 billion in revenue over the next year. But Anthropic’s growth rate already appears to be slowing, even as the company is projected to spend at least $450 billion in capital expenditures over the next four years. Goldman Sachs recently estimated that Anthropic won’t generate free cash flow—meaning make more than it spends—until 2030.

 The challenge for AI companies is to convince businesses in the rest of the economy to start spending massively on AI, and soon. Right now, despite the hype surrounding AI, that is not happening. A recent study by Torsten Slok, the chief economist at Apollo Global Management, found that spending on AI was highly concentrated in a small number of firms. Companies don’t want to scrap existing investments in favor of AI until the business case for it is clear (and perhaps not even then). For many CEOs, the benefits of paying for the latest frontier model—as opposed to older models, or even open-source ones—remain uncertain. Slok’s study found no sign that AI has boosted productivity growth outside of big tech firms.

 AI could still transform the economy. But this shift may be more of a long, drawn-out process—similar, perhaps, to the way electrification transformed American industry in the early 20th century—rather than a fast and dramatic one. Investors, though, have bet that the transformation will be rapid, as have Big Tech companies themselves. If it turns out to be a marathon rather than a sprint, lots of AI stocks will have been seriously overvalued—which may help to explain why those stocks have been selling off in recent weeks.

 Apart from what it might mean for your 401(k), this is not a bad development. If AI is indeed a bubble, letting the air out slowly is much better than having it burst all at once. The market is signaling to companies that the cash spigot will not be open forever and that if they can’t find ways to monetize the hundreds of billions of dollars they’re already pouring into data centers and computing power, then they need to slow down. Given that AI companies themselves keep talking about the potential existential risks this technology poses, a slowdown might well be beneficial—socially, economically, and otherwise.

 Although these companies have implicitly promised investors that they will become the most profitable in history, the problem now facing AI firms is ultimately the one that haunts nearly any for-profit enterprise: At some point, and probably sooner than they may like, they will have to show investors the money.
